4461               	; 		#if NES
4462               	; 		' A SECOND STAGING AREA, AND THIS IS THE WHOLE MARQUEE BUG.
4463               	; 		'
4464               	; 		' nes_escd does NOT copy anything. It builds the tile into the RAM
4465               	; 		' buffer `#nesb` and hands the NMI a five-byte descriptor holding a
4466               	; 		' POINTER to it; the copy happens at the next vblank. Both marquee
4467               	; 		' writes happen in the same pass, so with one buffer the darken call
4468               	; 		' overwrote the staged LIT bytes before the NMI had read either --
4469               	; 		' and then BOTH descriptors copied bulb_off.
4470               	; 		'
4471               	; 		' So every step darkened two lamps and lit none, and the sign walked
4472               	; 		' itself out: "it animates a little bit and goes out". Nothing fails,
4473               	; 		' because both writes are perfectly valid and land exactly where they
4474               	; 		' were addressed -- they just carry the same sixteen bytes.
4475               	; 		'
4476               	; 		' The lit call staged at nesb(0); this one stages sixteen bytes up.
4477               	; 		' nesb is 96 bytes for the escalator's six characters and the
4478               	; 		' escalator never runs on the title screen, so the room is free. The
4479               	; 		' pointer is put back immediately: esc_tick stages at offset 0 and
4480               	; 		' would otherwise write its six characters one tile off.
4481               	; 		#nesb = #nesb + 16
4482               	; 		#nsrc = VARPTR bulb_off(0)
4483               	; 		nchr = bcode
4484               	; 		ncnt = 1
4485               	; 		ntab = 1
4486               	; 		#ncol = 0
4487               	; 		nink = 3

4611               	; 	' 8-3-8 IS EDGE-TRIGGERED AND ANY STRAY DIGIT RESETS IT (see title_wait).

4616               	; 	' rather than a design, and it had two costs: 8,5,3,9,8 opened this page as

4621               	; 	' keyboard line -- and Classic99 defaults to invertcaps, so it reads DOWN
4622               	; 	' with the host's Caps Lock UP -- and this page was reached twice from
4623               	; 	' single keypresses while testing an unrelated change.

5042               	; 	' never reset when play began, so it carried its value in from whatever
5043               	; 	' happened last. Press FIRE on the title with jrel left at 1 and Kelly
5044               	; 	' jumps on the first frame of the round, having been told to do so by the
5045               	; 	' keypress that only meant "start".

5047               	; 	' It hid on the very first game of a session, because CVBasic zeroes its
5048               	; 	' variables and jrel = 0 already means "wait for a release" -- so it only
5049               	; 	' appeared on the SECOND round onwards, which reads as intermittent.
5050               	; 	'
5051               	; 	' start_krook is the one place worth doing this: new_game, losing a life
5052               	; 	' and advancing a Krook all pass through here, so every entry into play
5053               	; 	' demands a fresh press.

5060               	;
5061               	; 	' HARRY STARTS ON FLOOR 2 AT THE WEST EDGE OF SCREEN 7, and that is as
5062               	; 	' far left as the clock allows. The research says "the second-floor
5063               	; 	' elevator door", which is screen 3, and it cannot be done:
5064               	; 	'
5065               	; 	'   spawn      escape     round
5066               	; 	'   screen 3   119.9 s    100 s   -- impossible
5067               	; 	'   screen 5   108.1 s    100 s   -- impossible
5068               	; 	'   screen 6   102.3 s    100 s   -- impossible
5069               	; 	'   screen 7    96.4 s    100 s   -- 3.6 s of room
5070               	; 	'
5071               	; 	' HE STARTS AT THE LIFT NOW, AND THAT COST HIM A SPEED CHANGE.
5072               	; 	'
5073               	; 	' His escape route ZIGZAGS -- east along floor 2 to its escalator, WEST
5074               	; 	' along floor 3 to that one, then east again along the roof to the door.
5075               	; 	' From the lift on screen 3 that is 5,120 px against the 4,208 he walked
5076               	; 	' from screen 7, so at his old 1.75 px a pass he needed 105 s of a 100 s
5077               	; 	' round: he could never escape at all, and one of the two loss conditions
5078               	; 	' would quietly have stopped existing. This block used to say exactly that
5079               	; 	' and conclude the lift was impossible. It was impossible AT THAT SPEED.
5080               	; 	'
5081               	; 	' AND QUARTER-PIXELS COULD NOT EXPRESS THE ANSWER. A quarter of a pixel
5082               	; 	' per pass is worth about TEN SECONDS of his route, so the two candidate
5083               	; 	' values straddled the buzzer with nothing in between:
5084               	; 	'
5085               	; 	'   2.00 px/pass   escapes at 102.4 s of a 100 s round   never escapes
5086               	; 	'   2.25 px/pass   escapes at  91.0 s                    nine seconds early
5087               	; 	'
5088               	; 	' Worse, 2.25 was not reachable at all: the accumulator below had two
5089               	; 	' drain steps and therefore a hard ceiling of 2 px a pass, so hsp4 = 9
5090               	; 	' silently delivered 2.00 and he fell two thirds of a screen short of his
5091               	; 	' own escape. See the accumulator comment for the full account.
5092               	; 	'
5093               	; 	' Sixteenths with three drains put the step at about 2.5 s instead of 10,
5094               	; 	' and hsp64 = 35 (2.1875 px/pass) lands him at 96.3 s of the 100 --
5095               	; 	' escaping as the timer expires, which is what was asked for.
5096               	; 	'
5097               	; 	' 35 AND NOT 34, AND THE DIFFERENCE IS THE PLAYER'S OWN SCREEN. Measured
5098               	; 	' in play at 34: standing on an ordinary screen he escaped with one timer
5099               	; 	' unit left, and standing on the ELEVATOR screen he ran out of clock --

5335               	;
5336               	; 	' ======================================================================
5337               	; 	' DRAWING THE STORE -- four blits, once per screen crossing
5338               	; 	' ======================================================================
5339               	; 	' This is the whole cost of the flip, and it is paid on a discrete event
5340               	; 	' rather than every frame. RallyX's pan repaints 576 chars every time the
5341               	; 	' camera moves one cell; this repaints 640 about once every two seconds
5342               	; 	' of running.
5343               	; 	' SPRITES OFF BEFORE THE BLIT, NOT AFTER IT. This routine WAITs between
5344               	; 	' bands -- one band a frame, because a burst of VDP writes past a few
5345               	; 	' dozen in one frame is silently dropped -- so painting the new screen
5346               	; 	' takes several frames, and for all of them the OLD screen's actors and
5347               	; 	' obstacles were still sitting on top of it. Following Harry through a
5348               	; 	' seam showed him and every cart from the floor he had just left,
5349               	; 	' standing on a shop that was assembling itself underneath them.
5350               	; 	'
5351               	; 	' They are put back by the normal draw on the same pass, so the crossing
5352               	; 	' reads as a cut rather than as a dissolve with ghosts in it.
5353               	; 	' EACH BAND IS FINISHED BEFORE THE FRAME IT IS DRAWN IN ENDS, and the
5354               	; 	' bands go TOP DOWN. Both halves of that matter.
5355               	; 	'
5356               	; 	' The blit paints the template -- shelves, pillars and all -- and the
5357               	; 	' radios and prizes then take out the fixtures they stand in. Those two
5358               	; 	' used to be four frames apart: all four bands blitted with a WAIT
5359               	; 	' between them, and only afterwards the clearing. So every screen change
5360               	; 	' showed its counters and beams for several frames and then erased them,
5361               	; 	' which reads as the shop flickering rather than as it being drawn.
5362               	; 	'
5363               	; 	' TOP DOWN because a band's beam tops are stamped into the SLAB ROW OF
5364               	; 	' THE BAND ABOVE. Going bottom-up, band 1's blit would paint over the
5365               	; 	' beam tops band 0 had just put there. Going top-down the band above is
5366               	; 	' always already drawn, so everything a band needs -- its own cells and
5367               	; 	' the row it borrows overhead -- is final by the time its WAIT arrives.
5368               	; 	'
5369               	; 	' `3 - dq` rather than `FOR dlv = 3 TO 0 STEP -1`: dlv is an unsigned
5370               	; 	' byte, so counting down past zero wraps to 255 and the loop never ends
5371               	; 	' (CLAUDE.md 3A).
5372               	; draw_screen:
5373               cvb_DRAW_SCREEN
5374               	; 	#if NES
5375               	; 	' AND BLACK BACK FOR THE STORE -- see the note in title_draw. Index 0 is
5376               	; 	' the universal backdrop, so the dark blue the title sets would otherwise
5377               	; 	' tint every outline, the HUD row and the ground under the scanner.
5378               	; 	'
5379               	; 	' A DARK BLUE BACKDROP WAS TRIED HERE, to give the sunset a fourth band
5380               	; 	' (see nes_inkmap in assets/nes_chr.asm). It works, and it costs the
5381               	; 	' escalator, the radar ground and every black outline in the store, all of

5446               	; 		' ONE ROW A FRAME, AND THIS IS WHY THREE BANDS IN FOUR LOST THEIR
5447               	; 		' LAST TWO ROWS. The NMI copies PPUBUF into the PPU during vblank
5448               	; 		' and its copy loop DOES NOT STOP WHEN VBLANK ENDS -- it runs to
5449               	; 		' the end of the descriptor whatever the raster is doing, and a
5450               	; 		' PPUDATA write outside vblank is discarded by the hardware.
5451               	; 		'
5452               	; 		' NTSC gives about 2273 CPU cycles of vblank, OAM DMA takes 513 of
5453               	; 		' them, and the copy costs roughly 14 a byte: about a hundred bytes
5454               	; 		' get through. A 32x5 band is 160, so the last sixty-odd vanished
5455               	; 		' -- three whole rows arrived, the fourth stopped eight or nine
5456               	; 		' cells in, and the floor bar and the air row above it were simply
5457               	; 		' never there. Measured on screen as `#########.......`, on every
5458               	; 		' band whose blit did not happen to start early.
5459               	; 		'
5460               	; 		' A row is 32 bytes, which fits with room to spare. This costs four
5461               	; 		' extra frames per band at round start and nothing during play.
5462               	; 		FOR dsr = 0 TO 4
5463               	; 			SCREEN stor_tpl,#dsrc,#ddst,32,1,32
5464               	; 			#dsrc = #dsrc + 32
5465               	; 			#ddst = #ddst + 32
5466               	; 			WAIT
5467               	; 		NEXT dsr
5468               	; 		#else
5469               	; 		SCREEN stor_tpl,#dsrc,#ddst,32,5,32

5520               	; 	' A SUPPORT BEAM HAS TO REACH THE FLOOR IT HOLDS UP, AND THAT FLOOR IS
5521               	; 	' NOT IN ITS OWN BAND. A beam fills its band's four air rows, so its top
5522               	; 	' pixel sits under the slab row of the band ABOVE -- and a slab row is
5523               	; 	' five pixels of bar over three of green (see SLAB), so the beam stopped
5524               	; 	' three pixels short of the bar on every storey. It read as a beam that
5525               	; 	' misses the floor, which is exactly what it was.
5526               	; 	'
5527               	; 	' It cannot be drawn into either template. The beam belongs to the band
5528               	; 	' below and the row belongs to the band above, and the two templates are
5529               	; 	' chosen independently per screen, so no template knows both. So the
5530               	; 	' band blits go down first and the tops are stamped afterwards, from a
5531               	; 	' per-template column table -- the same shape as the escalator's head cap.
5532               	; 	'
5533               	; 	' Bands 0 and 1 only. Band 2's top row is the ROOF DECK, which is grey
5534               	; 	' over grey with no green to bridge, and the roof itself has no band
5535               	; 	' above it at all.
5536               	; 	' BANDS 0 TO 2 -- ALL THREE SHOPPING FLOORS. It used to stop at 1,
5537               	; 	' because band 2's ceiling is the ROOF DECK and the deck had no green

6051               	; 			' They read `IF lk = OB_RADIO THEN / IF krk < 2 THEN
6052               	; 			' lk = OB_BALL`, one per kind -- a hazard that had not
6053               	; 			' arrived was DOWNGRADED TO A BEACH BALL rather than
6054               	; 			' removed, so that a floor was never empty.
6055               	; 			'
6056               	; 			' That single decision is what the reviewer reported as
6057               	; 			' "you put balls on every screen on the 1st and 3rd
6058               	; 			' floors". On Krook 1 the radio, cart and plane all became
6059               	; 			' balls, and floors 0 and 2 had no occupancy gate at all,
6060               	; 			' so both carried one on every populated screen forever.
6061               	; 			' It was provable from the gates, not a tuning accident.
6062               	; 			' The original shows a MEDIAN OF ZERO hazards on level 1.
6063               	; 			'

6065               	; 			' write 0 -- which is the thing the gates could not say.)
6066               	; 			' (THE DOUBLING LADDER AND THE OCCUPANCY GATES STOOD HERE

6165               	; 			' from obk() instead, which is 8 bytes of RAM back and one
6166               	; 			' fewer thing that can disagree with itself.
6167               	; 			' THEY COME FROM THE FAR SIDE. Kelly walked into this screen
6168               	; 			' from one edge, so the obstacles start at the OTHER edge and
6169               	; 			' run toward him. Crossing a seam then always presents an
6170               	; 			' ONCOMING stream, never a set of backs he has to catch up
6171               	; 			' with -- and it means the direction he is travelling is
6172               	; 			' always the direction the danger comes from.
6173               	; 			'
6174               	; 			' The table's x becomes a stagger from that edge rather than
6175               	; 			' an absolute position, and the slot index spreads them out
6176               	; 			' so they arrive in sequence instead of as one wall.
6177               	; 			'
6178               	; 			' THE SECOND ONE IS A FIXED DISTANCE BEHIND THE FIRST, AND
6179               	; 			' THAT DISTANCE IS SET BY THE JUMP.
6180               	; 			'
6181               	; 			' It used to be `(lx AND 63) + 64` -- a masked byte out of
6182               	; 			' the placement table plus a constant -- so the gap between
6183               	; 			' the two hazards was whatever those two bytes happened to
6184               	; 			' differ by. Measured across the five populated screens it
6185               	; 			' came out 46, 46, 70, 70, 70 px. Screens 2 and 4 flank the
6186               	; 			' elevator, so the store had a visibly tighter pair on one
6187               	; 			' side of it than the other, which is exactly how it was
6188               	; 			' reported from play.
6189               	; 			'
6190               	; 			' Both numbers are too small, which is the real fault. Kelly
6191               	; 			' closes on an oncoming hazard at (KWALK64 + its speed)/64
6192               	; 			' px a FRAME, and the jump is airborne 28 frames, so a jump
6193               	; 			' eats 82 px of closing distance at the fastest hazard. At
6194               	; 			' 46 or 70 there is NO screen where he can land between the
6195               	; 			' two: he clears the first and comes down on the second.
6196               	; 			'
6197               	; 			' HAZGAP is that distance with margin, and it agrees with
6198               	; 			' the original to within 4 px (see the CONST). The pairing
6199               	; 			' is now a fact about the jump rather than an accident of
6200               	; 			' two bytes. assets/checkspace.py measures it and fails the
6201               	; 			' build.
6202               	; 			' THE SECOND SLOT IS MEASURED FROM THE FIRST, not from its
6203               	; 			' own table byte. Adding HAZGAP to its own `lx AND 63` would
6204               	; 			' still leave the GAP varying by up to 63 px between screens
6205               	; 			' -- the same fault in a politer form, and the reason the two
6206               	; 			' sides of the elevator differed in the first place. Holding
6207               	; 			' slot 0's stagger and adding to that makes the gap exactly
6208               	; 			' HAZGAP on every screen, while slot 0 still lands wherever
6209               	; 			' the table puts it, so the placement variety is untouched.
6210               	; 			' DERIVED FROM THE BAND, not stored. The table used to carry
6211               	; 			' an x byte per slot; slot 1's was ignored outright (it is
6212               	; 			' `stg0 + HAZGAP`) and slot 0's only reached the game as its
6213               	; 			' low six bits. `lix` is the band index, already in hand,
6214               	; 			' and three of it spreads the thirty-two bands across the

6311               	; 			' THE BALL IS ON THE GROUND WHEN HE GETS TO IT.
6312               	; 			'
6313               	; 			' The bounce phase used to be `lx AND 31` -- a byte out of
6314               	; 			' the placement table, which is to say arbitrary. Run onto
6315               	; 			' a screen and the first ball might be at the bottom of its
6316               	; 			' arc, where a jump clears it, or at the top, where it has
6317               	; 			' to be ducked, and nothing on the way in told you which.
6318               	; 			' Sometimes you could keep running and jump it; sometimes
6319               	; 			' the same approach at the same speed could not be jumped
6320               	; 			' at all. That is not difficulty, it is a coin toss.
6321               	; 			'
6322               	; 			' So the phase is worked BACKWARDS from the meeting. He
6323               	; 			' closes 4 px a pass and the ball 2, so they meet in
6324               	; 			' (gap / 6) passes; the phase advances one a pass and wraps
6325               	; 			' at 32, so seeding it with the NEGATIVE of that lands it on
6326               	; 			' phase 0 -- the ground -- exactly as they arrive.
6327               	; 			'
6328               	; 			' The gap is the same either way round: he enters at one
6329               	; 			' wall and the ball starts `stag` in from the other, so it
6330               	; 			' is 232 - stag whichever direction the floor runs.
6331               	; 			'
6332               	; 			' It stays forgiving rather than exact. The arc is flat near
6333               	; 			' the bottom, so anything within eight passes either side is
6334               	; 			' still under the jump; and it only holds for an unbroken
6335               	; 			' run, which is the case the player is entitled to read off
6336               	; 			' the screen. Duck, stop or take a hit and everything after
6337               	; 			' is out of step again -- which is the game.
6338               	; 			' obp is a BALL-only field: upd_obst reads it under an
6339               	; 			' IF uk = OB_BALL and nothing else touches it, and every
6340               	; 			' ball has it computed below. It was seeded here from a
6341               	; 			' table byte that no longer exists, and for anything but
6342               	; 			' a ball that seed was never read.

7317               	; 		' HE IS STANDING ON A STEP, so he moves at the STEP's rate: 2 px
7318               	; 		' across and 1 up PER PASS -- the staircase's own slope, and exactly
7319               	; 		' what one phase of esc_tick moves the pattern by.
7320               	; 		'
7321               	; 		' NOT `fdv`, WHICH IS THE WHOLE POINT. Everything else in this loop
7322               	; 		' is paced by the frame delta, and pacing him that way too made him
7323               	; 		' outrun the steps the moment a pass cost more than one frame: his
7324               	; 		' feet started planted on a tread and ended floating above it.
7325               	; 		' Pacing the ANIMATION by fdv instead is worse -- four phases cannot
7326               	; 		' be stepped by 2 or 3 without aliasing, and the staircase runs
7327               	; 		' backwards (see esc_tick). The only arrangement that cannot drift
7328               	; 		' is the one where both are driven by the same fixed step, so the
7329               	; 		' rider is clocked by the pass, like the steps he is standing on.
7330               	; 		'
7331               	; 		' THE FIRST FEW PASSES ARE THE STEP ON. Walking on, his feet are on
7332               	; 		' the floor and the bottom tread is 4 to 7 px above them, so he
7333               	; 		' climbs at 2 px a pass until he catches it (the tread is rising at
7334               	; 		' 1, so the gap closes at 1 a pass) and then rides with it. Jumping
7335               	; 		' on he lands ON a tread, so eson is 0 and this never runs.

7873               	; 		' a short step, it reads as the controls being ignored, and it is
7874               	; 		' worst exactly where a player taps rather than holds: lining up a
7875               	; 		' jump, or edging around a hazard.

7878               	; 		' fire. It does not cheat the RATE: the trigger subtracts fifteen
7879               	; 		' rather than zeroing, so the pixels actually travelled still carry
7880               	; 		' into the following step and a held run comes out at 6.9 a second

8817               	;
8818               	; 	' THE VICTROLA, AS CHARACTERS. It never moves, so a sprite spent a
8819               	; 	' scan-line slot on something that can be painted once when the screen is
8820               	; 	' drawn -- and at one 16x16 sprite it could only ever be one colour and
8821               	; 	' one size. Four cells is twice the area for no sprite at all.
8822               	; 	'
8823               	; 	' It stands ON the slab, so it fills the band's rows 2 and 3; row 4 is
8824               	; 	' the floor bar itself -- and a PRIZE uses those same two rows.
8825               	; 	'
8826               	; 	' THEY CAN SHARE A BAND, AND THE CLAIM THAT USED TO BE HERE WAS WRONG.
8827               	; 	' It said the two never share a screen because "genstore keeps prizes off
8828               	; 	' the screens that carry hazards". That stopped being true the moment
8829               	; 	' hazard placement moved into the per-Krook stor_lvl table, and nothing
8830               	; 	' noticed, because the prize table is not part of the level table and
8831               	; 	' every check was written about one object at a time. Two money bags ended
8832               	; 	' up standing on a radio -- not fighting it, since the two routines poke
8833               	; 	' different cells and the later writer simply wins, so they read as one
8834               	; 	' merged object.
8835               	; 	'
8836               	; 	' WHAT KEEPS THEM APART IS COLUMNS. A radio stands at column 7, 15 or 23
8837               	; 	' (see lrc below); genstore's _off_the_rack nudges a prize clear of all
8838               	; 	' three, and checklevels.py reads that arithmetic back out of THIS file
8839               	; 	' and fails the build on any overlap.
8840               	; 	'
8841               	; 	' rdall = 1 paints all four cells, 0 repaints only the top-right one --
8842               	; 	' the pulse. Same address arithmetic either way, so the two cannot drift.
8843               	; 	' A BEAM TOP HANGS OUT OF THE FLOOR ABOVE, and the beam it belongs to has
8844               	; 	' just been taken away. `beam_tops` stamps SLABP -- the floor bar with the
8845               	; 	' support carried up through its lower three pixel rows -- into the slab
8846               	; 	' row above every pillar, and it runs BEFORE the radios and prizes are
8847               	; 	' placed. Clearing a pillar's own cells therefore left three grey pixels
8848               	; 	' dangling from the ceiling with nothing under them.
8849               	; 	'
8850               	; 	' TESTED, NOT ASSUMED: only SLABP is put back to SLAB. The row above the
8851               	; 	' top shopping floor is the ROOF DECK, a different character altogether,
8852               	; 	' and writing a floor bar over it would punch a hole in the roof.
8853               	; 	' A SHELF RUN IS FIVE CELLS WIDE and a radio covers two, so one standing
8854               	; 	' on a counter punched a hole through its middle and left the ends either
8855               	; 	' side -- the same incoherence the dangling pillar had, and worse, because
8856               	; 	' a counter reads as one object. The whole unit goes: walk outward along
8857               	; 	' the band's row 2 while the cell is still a shelf top, clearing it and
8858               	; 	' its bottom half together.
8859               	; 	'
8860               	; 	' Bounded at eight steps. The runs are five, so eight is slack rather
8861               	; 	' than a guess -- and an unbounded walk would run off the end of the row
8862               	; 	' if the name table ever held something unexpected.
8863               	; 	#if NES
8864               	; 	' WHAT THE TEMPLATE PUT IN THIS CELL, for a target that cannot read its
8865               	; 	' own video memory back. #nta is the offset INSIDE the band (0-159) and
8866               	; 	' nbl is the band; the answer is the byte SCREEN blitted there.
8867               	; 	'
8868               	; 	' This is the same arithmetic the blit itself does in draw_band --
8869               	; 	' template id out of stor_ix for (band, screen), times 160, plus the
8870               	; 	' offset -- so the two cannot disagree about what is on screen. It is
8871               	; 	' reading what the cell MEANS, not guessing from where the cell is: a
8872               	; 	' coordinate is a fact about this layout, the character is a fact about
8873               	; 	' the world, and only the second is safe to erase on.
8874               	; nes_def:
8875               	; 	' WHAT DEFINE WOULD HAVE DONE. CVBasic implements no DEFINE at all for the
8876               	; 	' NES, on the reading that patterns live in cartridge CHR ROM -- but an
8877               	; 	' iNES header with a CHR-bank count of ZERO asks for 8 KB of CHR-RAM
8878               	; 	' instead, and that is the header CVBasic emits whenever the program uses
8879               	; 	' no BITMAP/CHRROM statement. So the pattern table here is ordinary VRAM
8880               	; 	' and this is the write. assets/nes_chr.asm carries the routine and the
8881               	; 	' reasoning; the caller sets #nsrc, nchr, ncnt and ntab.
8882               	; 	ASM JSR nes_chrup
8883               	; 	RETURN
8884               	;
8885               	; 	' AND THE SAME THING WITHOUT LOSING A FRAME. nes_def turns rendering off
8886               	; 	' and waits for a vblank the NMI therefore never services, so the game's
8887               	; 	' own WAIT then waits for the one after -- about two frames a call. That
8888               	; 	' is free at setup and ruinous anywhere that runs repeatedly. It builds
8889               	; 	' the same bytes into `nesb` and hands the NMI a single copy descriptor
8890               	; 	' instead. See assets/nes_chr.asm.
8891               	; 	'
8892               	; 	' THE NAME IS HISTORICAL: it was written for esc_tick, which redefines six
8893               	; 	' characters EVERY PASS on the two escalator screens and ran visibly slow
8894               	; 	' on nes_def. Nothing about it is escalator-specific -- it takes the same
8895               	; 	' inputs as nes_def plus #nesb, and the title's marquee uses it too, where
8896               	; 	' nes_def was switching the picture off twice a step and reading as a
8897               	; 	' flashing title screen.
8898               	; 	'
8899               	; 	' #nesb must point at a buffer of at least ncnt*16 bytes and is set once
8900               	; 	' in init_tables, which runs before boot: and therefore before the title.

9691               	; 	' THE BOUNCE PHASE, ON THE SAME CLOCK AS THE JUMP AND AT ITS OLD PERIOD.
9692               	; 	'
9693               	; 	' The jump has always advanced by the frame delta (`kjf = kjf + fdv`) while
9694               	; 	' the bounce advanced once per PASS -- so whether a jump cleared a ball
9695               	; 	' depended on how busy the screen was, and the frame-by-frame property
9696               	; 	' checkball.py proves was exact only at fdv = 1.
9697               	; 	'
9698               	; 	' Stepping the phase by fdv directly would fix the clock and wreck the
9699               	; 	' game: a 32-phase arc would drop from about 1.35 s to 0.55 s, balls
9700               	; 	' bouncing 2.4x faster everywhere. So it gets a fraction of its own --
9701               	; 	' 25/64 of a phase per frame is 23.4 phases a second, against the 23.8 it
9702               	; 	' runs at today. Same bounce, now the same clock as the thing that has to
9703               	; 	' clear it.

9949               	; 	' ONE STEP OF A FRACTIONAL SPEED, FOR WHOEVER IS MOVING.
9950               	; 	'
9951               	; 	' `pacc` in and out, `psp64` in (sixty-fourths of a pixel per FRAME),
9952               	; 	' `pspd` out (whole pixels this pass). CVBasic has no locals, so the caller
9953               	; 	' stages its own accumulator in and takes it back out; that costs four
9954               	; 	' statements against the fourteen this used to be, written out per actor.
9955               	; 	'
9956               	; 	' Harry had the only copy. Kelly, the hazards and the bounce phase all need
9957               	; 	' the same thing -- everything the round clock judges has to advance by
9958               	; 	' ELAPSED FRAMES, or the loop rate becomes a difficulty dial and where the
9959               	; 	' player stands decides the outcome (DESIGN.md 0f-ter).
9960               	; 	'
9961               	; 	' TWO DRAINS CAP THE STEP AT 2 PER FRAME whatever psp64 says (CLAUDE.md
9962               	; 	' 3A: N drains cap the speed at N, and the surplus leaks into a byte that
9963               	; 	' wraps). Every caller is under that: Kelly 102/64 = 1.6, the fastest
9964               	; 	' hazard 76/64 = 1.2, Harry 57/64 = 0.9, the bounce phase 25/64 = 0.4.
9965               	; 	'
9966               	; 	' FIVE FRAMES, AND THREE WAS TOO FEW. At 2 px a frame five frames is 10 px,
9967               	; 	' and to skip a position window an actor must start outside it on one side
9968               	; 	' and land outside on the other, which needs 12. Three was the original bug
9969               	; 	' in miniature: the lift screen runs at almost exactly 20 passes a second,
9970               	; 	' which IS fdv = 3, so every hitch there lost a frame. The clamp exists for
9971               	; 	' a genuine stall and at five it only fires for one.

10459               	;
10460               	; 	' THE SIXTEENTH-PIXEL ACCUMULATOR. hx is one unsigned byte per screen
10461               	; 	' (2), so there is nowhere to keep a fraction -- the fraction lives here
10462               	; 	' and is spent as whole pixels. THREE IFs, not a loop and not a divide:
10463               	; 	' `%` and `/` both compile to a real TMS9900 DIV (CLAUDE.md 3A) and this
10464               	; 	' runs every pass.
10465               	; 	'
10466               	; 	' THE NUMBER OF DRAINS IS A CEILING ON THE SPEED, AND THAT IS THE WHOLE
10467               	; 	' POINT OF THIS COMMENT. Each IF can spend one whole pixel, so N drains
10468               	; 	' cap hspd at N px per pass NO MATTER WHAT hsp64 SAYS. The invariant is:
10469               	; 	'
10470               	; 	'     hacc is under 16 on entry, and hsp64 is at most 48,
10471               	; 	'     so hacc is under 64 here and three drains always suffice.
10472               	; 	'
10473               	; 	' KEEP hsp64 <= 48. This was quarter-pixels with TWO drains and the same
10474               	; 	' invariant written the same way -- "hsp4 is at most 8, so it can never
10475               	; 	' need a third" -- and it was correct until somebody set hsp4 = 9 without
10476               	; 	' re-reading it. The crook then ran at a flat 2.0 px/pass while every
10477               	; 	' comment, the design table and assets/checkchase.py all said 2.25, and
10478               	; 	' the surplus quarter leaked into hacc and wrapped the byte every 256
10479               	; 	' passes. Nothing failed; he simply arrived two thirds of a screen short
10480               	; 	' of his own escape. checkchase.py now counts these IFs and refuses a
10481               	; 	' speed the drains cannot deliver.
10482               	; 	'
10483               	; 	' 7, NOT 6, AND THE REASON IS MEASURED. Tracked off the reference video
10484               	; 	' (DESIGN.md 4a), the 2600's Kelly covers 0.40 screen widths a second and
10485               	; 	' its Harry 0.193 -- a ratio of 2.07. At hsp4 = 6 ours was 2.67, and the
10486               	; 	' crook visibly strolled. 7 brings it to 2.29. 8 would match the original
10487               	; 	' exactly and cannot be used: Kelly's route here is 1.95x Harry's, so a
10488               	; 	' speed ratio of 2.0 leaves the on-foot chase 0.2 s of slack, which is no
10489               	; 	' chase at all. checkchase.py holds the line.
10490               	; 	' STILL RUNNING FROM THE STAIRS -- and this has to come BEFORE the move,
10491               	; 	' not after it. It sat below the two `IF hmv` blocks, where all it could
10492               	; 	' still reach was the animation counter: he faced the right way, played
10493               	; 	' the run cycle and did not travel a pixel. He stood at the foot of the
10494               	; 	' flight looking busy.
10495               	; 	'
10496               	; 	' TWO THINGS END THE RUN, AND BOTH ARE VISIBLE ON SCREEN.
10497               	; 	'
10498               	; 	' THE KOP ARRIVING ON THIS FLOOR OUTRANKS IT. This used to override the

10501               	; 	' appearing to notice he was there. The flee above has already worked out

10503               	; 	'

10590               	;
10591               	; 	' HE WALKS BY REAL TIME, NOT BY LOOP PASS -- one accumulate-and-drain per
10592               	; 	' ELAPSED FRAME rather than per pass. Everything that moves here used to be
10593               	; 	' per pass while the CLOCK is paced by the frame delta, so a busy screen
10594               	; 	' slowed Harry in real seconds and the clock did not slow with him: the
10595               	; 	' same uninterrupted escape finished with nine timer units in hand from a
10596               	; 	' light screen and none at all from the lift screen, decided by where the
10597               	; 	' player happened to be standing. Now he covers the same ground per second
10598               	; 	' wherever anybody is (DESIGN.md 0f-ter).
10599               	; 	'
10600               	; 	' A LOOP, NOT A MULTIPLY. `*` compiles to a real TMS9900 MPY, and reading a
10601               	; 	' 16-bit variable straight after one returns the product's HIGH word
10602               	; 	' (CLAUDE.md 3A). fdv is 1..3 here, so this is at most three adds.
10603               	; 	'
10604               	; 	' SIXTY-FOURTHS, AND ONLY TWO DRAINS -- both fall out of accumulating per
10605               	; 	' FRAME instead of per pass. He covers under a pixel a frame, so two drains
10606               	; 	' are ample where the per-pass version needed three; and the finer unit is
10607               	; 	' what makes the speed tunable at all. In sixteenths one step was about six
10608               	; 	' SECONDS of his route, so nothing landed near the buzzer; in sixty-fourths
10609               	; 	' it is about one and a half. Keep hsp64 <= 128: hacc is under 64 on entry,
10610               	; 	' so 64 + 128 stays inside a byte and two drains always suffice.
10611               	; 	'
10612               	; 	' AND THE STEP IS CLAMPED TO THREE FRAMES' WORTH, WHICH IS NOT A DETAIL.
10613               	; 	' Two tests sample his position once a pass and neither interpolates:
10614               	; 	'
10615               	; 	'   ARRIVAL   `hdx < 6` around the escalator or the roof door -- an ELEVEN
10616               	; 	'             pixel window. A step over 10 px can jump clean across it and
10617               	; 	'             he never arrives at all.
10618               	; 	'   THE CATCH `hdd < CATCHR` is 12, a 23-wide band, and Kelly closes 4 of
10619               	; 	'             it himself -- so Harry over ~18 px could pass through the Kop
10620               	; 	'             between two passes without either sample being inside it.
10621               	; 	'
10622               	; 	' The clamp and the drains live in pace_step now, with the reasoning; the
10623               	; 	' numbers above are what sized them. Measured: TIME 02 on the lift screen
10624               	; 	' against TIME 04 on a light one when the clamp was 3, and 00 against 09
10625               	; 	' before any of this.
10626               	; 	'
10627               	; 	' The ESCALATOR RIDE is deliberately untouched: it returns above this,
10628               	; 	' clocked one step per pass to stay locked to the moving staircase. A rider
10629               	; 	' advanced by the frame delta either drifts off the treads or makes the

11096               	;
11097               	; 	' ======================================================================
11098               	; 	' COLLISIONS -- pure arithmetic against RAM, no VDP reads
11099               	; 	' ======================================================================
11100               	; 	' Kelly's box is [kfh, kfh + kh) above the slab; an obstacle's is
11101               	; 	' [ohb, oht). The ball's inset hitbox is what makes 8..10 avoidable both
11102               	; 	' ways -- without it there is a height at which the ball can be neither
11103               	; 	' jumped nor ducked, and an unavoidable hazard is not difficulty.
11104               	; 	' ONE HIT PER CONTACT, WITH A REFRACTORY PERIOD.
11105               	; 	'
11106               	; 	' The overlap test is true on every frame the player is touching
11107               	; 	' something, so with no latch at all one clumsy cart charges nine seconds
11108               	; 	' several times over -- and what the player sees is the clock jumping by
11109               	; 	' 27, from which the only available conclusion is that the penalty is
11110               	; 	' broken.
11111               	; 	'
11112               	; 	' A latch that clears on the first non-overlapping frame is still not
11113               	; 	' enough, and the case that breaks it is the BOUNCING BALL: it rises off
11114               	; 	' the player between bounces, which is a genuine loss of contact, so a
11115               	; 	' player standing still under one is taxed on every single bounce while
11116               	; 	' being given no opportunity to do anything about it. Technically two
11117               	; 	' collisions; in play, one situation.
11118               	; 	'
11119               	; 	' So obht() is a countdown, not a flag. A hit sets it to HITREF; it ticks
11120               	; 	' down only while the player is CLEAR, and the same obstacle cannot charge
11121               	; 	' again until it reaches zero. Contact holds the count up, so parking
11122               	; 	' inside something never earns a second penalty either.
11123               	; coll_obst:
11124               cvb_COLL_OBST

11490               	; 	' THE FLOOR CLEARS WHEN YOU ARE HIT, and stays clear until you re-enter
11491               	; 	' the screen. Nine seconds is a heavy penalty on a fifty-unit clock, and
11492               	; 	' taking it while still standing among the things that charged it -- with
11493               	; 	' a second hazard 48 px behind the first -- is how one mistake becomes
11494               	; 	' three. Clearing the row makes the penalty a single event you can walk
11495               	; 	' away from.
11496               	; 	'

11679               	; 	' AND THEY HAVE TO BE AT THE SAME HEIGHT, NOT MERELY ON THE SAME FLOOR.
11680               	; 	'
11681               	; 	' `hlv` does not change until a ride ENDS -- a crook stepping onto a
11682               	; 	' flight keeps the floor he left until he arrives at the next one. So
11683               	; 	' while he was most of a storey up or down the stairs he still counted as
11684               	; 	' standing on the floor he started from, and a Kop who ran over the head
11685               	; 	' of the flight arrested him through the floor. Reported from play:
11686               	; 	' "I run over top of him, even though we do not touch".
11687               	; 	'
11688               	; 	' It is the same shape of bug as the catch that fired at MAXIMUM
11689               	; 	' separation: a test that is right about one axis and silent about the
11690               	; 	' other, where the silent one happens to be true nearly all the time.
11691               	; 	'
11692               	; 	' UNSIGNED-SAFE. Riding up is above the shared floor and riding down is
11693               	; 	' below it, which is a signed quantity, and CVBasic's variables are not.
11694               	; 	' So both are collected as POSITIVE heights on opposite sides -- Kelly's
11695               	; 	' climb plus Harry's descent on one side, Harry's climb on the other --
11696               	; 	' and the difference is taken between two numbers that cannot go
11697               	; 	' negative. Two riders passing on the same flight measure the sum of
11698               	; 	' their heights, which is exactly the distance between them.

11808               	; 	' CVBasic's SPRITE writes a RAM mirror which the vblank ISR copies to

12027               	; 		' FOUR RUN FRAMES FROM TWO BITS of the animation counter, and no
12028               	; 		' divide -- `/` compiles to a real TMS9900 DIV (CLAUDE.md 3A) and
12029               	; 		' this is per-frame code. Two adjacent bits give 0,4,8,12.
12030               	; 		'
12031               	; 		' KELLY USES BITS 2 AND 3 AND HARRY USES 3 AND 4, because a stride
12032               	; 		' has to cover about a stride's worth of ground or the figure
12033               	; 		' skates. Kelly runs 4 px a frame, so four frames a pose is 16 px;
12034               	; 		' Harry runs 1.75, so eight frames a pose is 14. Matching the two
12035               	; 		' rates to the two speeds is what keeps both looking like running.
12036               	; 		' ONE PATTERN FOR THE WHOLE BODY. This picked a leg frame here and
12037               	; 		' a tunic twenty lines below, and drew them as two sprites. The
12038               	; 		' merged run bodies carry both, so the two ladders are one and the
12039               	; 		' fourth SPRITE call is gone.

12375               	; 	' HE IS STRIPED FROM CAP TO HEM. Both stripe colours run the whole upper
12376               	; 	' half, so both boxes span rows 0-15 and neither can be tucked away --
12377               	; 	' affordable only because Kelly's hat moved into a box of its own. His
12378               	; 	' FACE is pushed DOWN instead (hy+3, box 3..18) so it clears the cap
12379               	; 	' rows, where his two stripe boxes plus Kelly's hat and face already
12380               	; 	' make four. Worst line of a meeting: exactly four, nothing dropped.
12381               	; 	' HE RISES A PIXEL ON THE RECOVERY BEATS. A runner is highest at mid-flight
12382               	; 	' and lowest at contact; with the body pinned at a constant y, alternating
12383               	; 	' legs under a motionless torso reads as a dance rather than as travel.
12384               	; 	'
12385               	; 	' One pixel is enough at this size, and it lifts the BODY ONLY -- the legs
12386               	; 	' keep their y, so the planted foot stays on the floor and the figure
12387               	; 	' stretches at the waist instead of hopping. Lifting the legs too would be
12388               	; 	' a jump.
12389               	; 	'
12390               	; 	' Beats 2 and 4 are the recoveries, which is exactly `hanim AND 8` -- the
12391               	; 	' cycle's LOW beat bit. IT MUST MOVE WITH THE BEAT BITS ABOVE IT: on the
12392               	; 	' wrong bit he rises and falls twice per stride, a second clock inside one
12393               	; 	' figure, which is the flapping of DESIGN.md 0j2 in the vertical.
12394               	; 	'
12395               	; 	' Safe because HARRY'S COLLISION HAS NO VERTICAL COMPONENT: he is caught on
12396               	; 	' `same level AND |dx| < CATCHR`. Doing this to Kelly would desynchronise

12868               	; 	' ======================================================================
12869               	; 	' THE SCANNER
12870               	; 	' ======================================================================
12871               	; 	' Rows 21-23, 16 chars wide, centred: 48 characters whose PATTERNS are
12872               	; 	' poked directly, so a moving dot costs two writes and no name-table
12873               	; 	' traffic. With the flip (DESIGN.md 2a) this is how you know where Harry
12874               	; 	' is at all -- he can be one pixel off-screen and completely invisible.
12875               	; 	'
12876               	; 	' Rows 21-23 all sit in the THIRD screen third, so every scanner pattern
12877               	; 	' is at base 4096 and no third-selection arithmetic is needed.
12878               	; 	'
12879               	; 	' BOTH DOTS ARE WHITE and Kelly's BLINKS. The manual wants Kelly black
12880               	; 	' and Harry white, but this is the TMS9918's two-colours-per-8x1-cell
12881               	; 	' mode: a black dot and a white dot on the same pixel row of the same
12882               	; 	' character cannot both exist. Blinking distinguishes them with one
12883               	; 	' colour, which is what RallyX does with its player dot.
12884               	; 	' THE STEPS MOVE, AND EVERY ESCALATOR ON SCREEN MOVES WITH THEM. A flight
12885               	; 	' is twelve characters -- six per direction, sliced out of a rendered
12886               	; 	' 64x40 bitmap by genart.py -- so rewriting those twelve PATTERNS animates
12887               	; 	' the lot: 96 bytes, no name-table traffic, and the same cost whether one
12888               	; 	' flight is visible or ten. The phases slide the cells ALONG the slope, so
12889               	; 	' the steps travel up the flight rather than drifting sideways.
12890               	; esc_tick:
12891               cvb_ESC_TICK
12892               	; 	' ONLY SCREENS 0 AND 7 CARRY A FLIGHT, so six screens in eight skip this
12893               	; 	' entirely -- which is what makes rewriting the cells every frame
12894               	; 	' affordable. Nested, not `klsc > 0 AND klsc < 7`: the 9900 backend
12895               	; 	' miscompiles a compare-AND-compare (CLAUDE.md 3A).
12896               	; 	IF klsc > 0 THEN

12915               	; 	' ONE PHASE PER PASS, AND NEVER MORE. There are four phases covering an
12916               	; 	' 8 px period, so advancing by the frame delta ALIASES: at fdv 2 the
12917               	; 	' pattern flips between two positions half a period apart and the
12918               	; 	' direction stops being readable, and at fdv 3 the sequence runs 0,3,2,1
12919               	; 	' -- the staircase visibly runs BACKWARDS, carrying its steps down while
12920               	; 	' the rider goes up. That is the wagon-wheel effect, and no amount of
12921               	; 	' phase arithmetic fixes it: a 4-phase cycle can only be stepped by 1.
12922               	; 	'
12923               	; 	' So the ANIMATION is the clock here, and the rider is paced from it --
12924               	; 	' see move_kelly, which advances him by the same fixed 2-and-1 per pass
12925               	; 	' rather than by fdv. Locking the two together is the only way they
12926               	; 	' cannot drift, and it is what "the player moves at the rate the steps
12927               	; 	' carry him" actually means. The cost is that a ride takes 36 passes
12928               	; 	' rather than 36 frames, so it slows down when the loop does -- which is
12929               	; 	' the honest behaviour for a machine that is carrying you.

13261               	;
13262               	; 	' ------------------------------------------------- the scanner's furniture
13263               	; 	' Without this the scanner is two dots in a void: you can see THAT Harry is
13264               	; 	' somewhere, but not what he is near, which is the one thing you actually
13265               	; 	' need when he is off-screen. Floor lines say which level, the slashes say
13266               	; 	' where that floor's escalator is, and the bar says where the elevator is --
13267               	; 	' exactly the three things the manual lists.
13268               	; 	'
13269               	; 	' FURNITURE AND DOTS ARE SEGREGATED BY PIXEL ROW ON PURPOSE, and a level
13270               	; 	' band is now FOUR rows, one per colour, because a pixel row carries
13271               	; 	' exactly one colour here:
13272               	; 	'
13273               	; 	'   +0  GREY    escalator head, and the elevator car
13274               	; 	'   +1  GREY    the air of that floor
13275               	; 	'   +2  GREY
13276               	; 	'   +3  YELLOW  the floor line -- and NOTHING else goes here
13277               	; 	'
13278               	; 	' THE FIRST THREE ROWS ARE THE FLOOR'S AIR AND EVERYTHING LIVES IN THEM:
13279               	; 	' the escalator's three-step diagonal, the lift car, and both actors, all
13280               	; 	' three pixels tall. They are grey in the table, and the Kop and the
13281               	; 	' crook recolour their own CHARACTER as they move (scan_mark) -- which is
13282               	; 	' what lets both of them fill the band instead of getting a pixel row
13283               	; 	' each. Eight pixels of this canvas is half a screen of the store, so
13284               	; 	' they are almost never in one character; when they are, they merge.
13285               	; 	'
13286               	; 	' Shrinking from six rows bought eight empty pixel rows, four above the
13287               	; 	' instrument and four below, so it no longer butts against the shop floor
13288               	; 	' above it or the bottom of the screen.
13289               	; 	'
13290               	; 	' The dots are erased by ANDing their bits out, so anything sharing a row
13291               	; 	' with one is rubbed away wherever an actor has passed -- which is why
13292               	; 	' scan_escs and scan_elev redraw every tick rather than once.
13293               	; scan_furn:

13679               	;
13680               	; 	' Blank the canvas by WRITING zeros rather than copying 384 of them out
13681               	; 	' of ROM. This runs twice a game -- at setup and on a new Krook -- so a
13682               	; 	' loop costs nothing anybody can perceive, and it hands the fixed area
13683               	; 	' back the best part of half a kilobyte, which is the budget that
13684               	; 	' actually binds. Paced in bursts: a few hundred VDP writes in a single
13685               	; 	' frame are silently dropped (CLAUDE.md 3A).
13686               	; scan_wipe:
13687               cvb_SCAN_WIPE
13688               	; 	' THIS ADDRESS IS A CHARACTER CODE IN DISGUISE, AND IT WENT STALE.
13689               	; 	' 4096 is the pattern table's BOTTOM THIRD -- rows 16-23, which is
13690               	; 	' band 0 and the radar together -- and the canvas characters begin at
13691               	; 	' genart's SCAN_FIRST, so the base is 4096 + SCAN_FIRST*8. It was
13692               	; 	' written out by hand as 4096 + 160*8 when SCAN_FIRST was 160; art
13693               	; 	' added later moved SCAN_FIRST to 208 and nothing moved this with it,
13694               	; 	' so the wipe zeroed the 48 characters BELOW the canvas and never
13695               	; 	' touched the canvas at all.
13696               	; 	'
13697               	; 	' Two of those forty-eight are STRUCTURE. ENDWALL is the building's
13698               	; 	' outside wall and SLABP is a pillar's cap. Blanking a pattern in ONE
13699               	; 	' THIRD leaves a character that draws correctly everywhere else and
13700               	; 	' falls back to its own background colour here -- so the GROUND FLOOR's
13701               	; 	' outside wall turned into plain green while the identical wall one
13702               	; 	' storey up was perfect, and the ground floor's pillars lost the brick
13703               	; 	' carried up through the bar above them. ENDWALL appears only on
13704               	; 	' screens 0 and 7, which is exactly why it was reported as happening
13705               	; 	' only on the escalator screens, mirrored side to side.
13706               	; 	'
13707               	; 	' The name table was correct the whole time. Probing it said so, four
13708               	; 	' times. It was the GLYPH that was empty, in one third only -- which a
13709               	; 	' probe that copies the character somewhere else to look at it cannot
13710               	; 	' see, because the copy renders from a different third's pattern.
13711               	; 	'
13712               	; 	' renumber.py rewrites this line from genart.SCAN_FIRST, and
13713               	; 	' checkstruct.py fails the build if the two disagree.
13714               	; 	#swa = 5760			' 4096 + SCAN_FIRST*8, the canvas patterns
13715 F0CE 0200  20 	li r0,5760
     F0D0 1680     
13716 F0D2 C800  38 	mov r0,@cvb__SWA
     F0D4 20EE     
13717               	; 	#if NES
13718               	; 	' AN NES TILE IS SIXTEEN BYTES, NOT EIGHT -- two bitplanes. DERIVED FROM
13719               	; 	' THE LINE ABOVE rather than written out again: renumber.py rewrites that
13720               	; 	' literal out of genart.SCAN_FIRST and checkstruct.py checks it, and a
13721               	; 	' second hand-kept copy of the same number is exactly the fault recorded
13722               	; 	' in the comment above this routine.
13723               	; 	#swa = #swa + #swa
13724               	; 	#swa = #swa - 4096
13725               	; 	#endif
13726               	; 	' THE SHADOW TAKES ITS BASE FROM THE LINE ABOVE, never from a second
13727               	; 	' copy of the number. renumber.py rewrites that literal out of
13728               	; 	' genart.SCAN_FIRST, and a hand-kept duplicate of it is precisely the
13729               	; 	' fault recorded in the comment above -- one copy moved, the other did
13730               	; 	' not, and the wipe spent months clearing the wrong forty-eight
13731               	; 	' characters. 6 x 64 is 384, which is the size of nsc.
13732               	; 	#if NES
13733               	; 	#nsb = #swa
13734               	; 	#nsi = 0
13735               	; 	#endif
13736               	; 	#if NES
13737               	; 	' TWELVE BURSTS, NOT SIX: 48 tiles of SIXTEEN bytes. The shadow is indexed
13738               	; 	' by the same offset the PPU address uses, so it grows with the stride --
13739               	; 	' half of what it holds is the second bitplane, which this port never sets
13740               	; 	' and scan_or1 therefore never reads as ink.
13741               	; 	' AND THE CANVAS IS WIPED TO GREEN, NOT TO BLACK.
13742               	; 	'
13743               	; 	' On the TI a blank canvas is zeros and the COLOUR TABLE says what the
13744               	; 	' background is. There is no colour table here: a pixel's colour is its
13745               	; 	' two bitplane bits, so "green background" means plane 0 SET everywhere
13746               	; 	' and plane 1 clear -- index 1, which is the store's green in P0.
13747               	; 	'
13748               	; 	' THAT INVERTS THE SENSE OF EVERY FEATURE DRAWN ON TOP. The floor lines
13749               	; 	' add plane 1 to reach index 3 (gold), and the escalator diagonals CLEAR
13750               	; 	' plane 0 to reach index 0 (the backdrop, black) -- see scan_or1, which
13751               	; 	' is why it ANDs here and ORs on the TI. Writing zeros here instead would
13752               	; 	' leave the instrument black-on-black and the flights invisible.
13753               	; 	'
13754               	; 	' A tile is sixteen bytes: 0-7 are plane 0 and 8-15 plane 1, so the byte's
13755               	; 	' position within its tile decides which it is.
13756               	; 	' AND THE MARGINS ARE GREY, WHICH IS THE OTHER BITPLANE PAIR.
13757               	; 	'
13758               	; 	' The canvas is three character rows -- 24 pixel rows -- of which the
13759               	; 	' instrument uses the middle SIXTEEN (rows 4-19: four levels of four).
13760               	; 	' The outer eight are deliberate air, four above and four below, so the
13761               	; 	' radar does not butt against the shop floor above it or the screen edge
13762               	; 	' below. On the TI those rows take the scanner's own background; here they
13763               	; 	' are index 2, the store's grey, against the instrument's green.
13764               	; 	'
13765               	; 	' Two bitplanes give the four colours this canvas needs and nothing else
13766               	; 	' has to change: index 1 green is plane 0, index 2 grey is plane 1, and
13767               	; 	' the floor lines and flights work on top of those (scan_furn, scan_or1).
13768               	; 	'
13769               	; 	' The byte's place in the canvas says which it is. 256 bytes is one
13770               	; 	' CHARACTER row (16 tiles of 16), the low three bits are the pixel row
13771               	; 	' within the tile, and bit 3 of the position picks the bitplane.
13772               	; 	FOR swj = 0 TO 11

13777               	; 			swm = 0

13780               	; 			END IF

13783               	; 			END IF

13785               	; 				' grey: plane 1 set, plane 0 clear

13787               	; 					swv = 255
13788               	; 				ELSE
13789               	; 					swv = 0
13790               	; 				END IF
13791               	; 			ELSE
13792               	; 				' green: plane 0 set, plane 1 clear
13793               	; 				IF swv > 7 THEN
13794               	; 					swv = 0
13795               	; 				ELSE
13796               	; 					swv = 255

13874               	; 	' THE TWO ACTORS ARE SPRITES; EVERYTHING ELSE IS CHARACTERS.
13875               	; 	'
13876               	; 	' That split is what makes the instrument simple. The floor lines, the
13877               	; 	' flights and the lift car do not move relative to the canvas, so they
13878               	; 	' are pixels in the scanner's own characters and cost nothing to keep.
13879               	; 	' The Kop and the crook DO move, and as sprites they need no colour
13880               	; 	' table, no erase and no priority arithmetic -- they draw over the
13881               	; 	' furniture because sprites always do, and nothing shifts to make room.
13882               	; 	'
13883               	; 	' IT ALSO REMOVED THE BLINK. Kelly flashed because a pixel row of this
13884               	; 	' canvas can only carry one colour, so at close range the two markers
13885               	; 	' merged and the blink was the only thing left to tell them apart. Two
13886               	; 	' sprites are two colours wherever they stand.
13887               	; 	'
13888               	; 	' The furniture is drawn ONCE, by scan_furn. It used to be redrawn every
13889               	; 	' tick because erasing a character-based marker ANDed bits out of
13890               	; 	' whatever it was standing on; there is nothing left to rub it away. The
13891               	; 	' car still redraws itself, because the car actually moves.
13892               	; 	' -- the lift car. IT WAS FLICKERING, and the cause was not the drawing
13893               	; 	' but the ERASING: scan_elev cleared its three cells and put them back
13894               	; 	' every tick, whether or not the car had moved, so several times a second
13895               	; 	' there was a window with the pixels off. A sprite has no erase at all --
13896               	; 	' it is placed, and the VDP does the rest -- and slot 26 sits BELOW the

14280               	;
14281               	; #if NES
14282               	; 	' ----------------------------------------------------------------------
14283               	; 	' THE ATTRIBUTE TABLE -- the NES's only way of giving two parts of the
14284               	; 	' screen different colours.
14285               	; 	'
14286               	; 	' 64 bytes at $23C0. Each byte covers FOUR character rows and four
14287               	; 	' columns, split into four 2x2 quadrants of two bits each: bits 0-1 top
14288               	; 	' left, 2-3 top right, 4-5 bottom left, 6-7 bottom right.
14289               	; 	'
14290               	; 	' The picture sits three rows down for overscan, which lands the regions
14291               	; 	' on block boundaries almost by luck:
14292               	; 	'
14293               	; 	'   byte row 0   name rows 0-3    the HUD is row 3  -> bottom quads P1
14294               	; 	'   byte row 1   name rows 4-7    the sky, top half -> P2, bottom -> P3
14295               	; 	'   byte rows 2+ name rows 8-29   the store         -> P0
14296               	; 	'
14297               	; 	' $50 is "bottom two quadrants on palette 1"; $FA is "top two on palette
14298               	; 	' 2, bottom two on palette 3", which is what splits the sunset into a
14299               	; 	' blue band over a warm one. Written as bare literals because this is the
14300               	; 	' one place the bit layout is visible, and naming them would hide it.
14301               	; 	'
14302               	; 	' 64 VPOKEs is 192 bytes of PPU queue, and WRTVRM waits when the 64-byte
14303               	; 	' buffer fills, so this paces itself across three frames and cannot
14304               	; 	' overrun vblank the way a single big SCREEN blit can.
14305               	; nes_attr:
14306               	; 	#nav = 9152			' $23C0
14307               	; 	FOR nai = 0 TO 7
14308               	; 		VPOKE #nav,80
14309               	; 		#nav = #nav + 1
14310               	; 	NEXT nai
14311               	; 	FOR nai = 0 TO 7
14312               	; 		VPOKE #nav,170			' $AA -- the whole sky band on P2, no second palette
14313               	; 		#nav = #nav + 1
14314               	; 	NEXT nai
14315               	; 	FOR nai = 0 TO 47
14316               	; 		VPOKE #nav,0
14317               	; 		#nav = #nav + 1
14318               	; 	NEXT nai
14319               	; 	RETURN
14320               	; #endif
14321               	;
14322               	; 	' Repeated subtraction rather than a divide: four steps, cheaper than a
14323               	; 	' DIV on this CPU, and only run when the value actually changes.

14766               	;
14767               	; 	' THE BONUS IS COUNTED OUT, NOT AWARDED. Dropping the whole sum into the
14768               	; 	' score in one frame tells the player a number; ticking the clock down a
14769               	; 	' unit at a time, with the score climbing and a beat under each step,
14770               	; 	' tells them what the number was FOR. It is the pay-off for every second
14771               	; 	' they saved, and every arcade game of this era spends a moment on it.
14772               	; 	'
14773               	; 	' It also costs nothing to get right: the loop already has to run down
14774               	; 	' `tsec`, so the animation IS the calculation, and the repeated-addition
14775               	; 	' note below stops applying -- each step adds one band's worth.
14776               	; 	'
14777               	; 	' x100 for Krooks 1-9, x200 for 10-15, x300 from 16. Two independent
14778               	; 	' sources agree on those bands; the manual's own wording suggests
14779               	; 	' 1-8 / 9-16 / 17+ and DESIGN.md 0 records the disagreement.
14780               	; 	'
14781               	; 	' IN UNITS OF TEN, WHICH IS WHAT THE SCORE IS COUNTED IN, so the bands are
14782               	; 	' 10 / 20 / 30 and not 100 / 200 / 300.
14783               	; 	'
14784               	; 	' They were 100 / 200 / 300 and paid TEN TIMES the right bonus -- 1,000 a
14785               	; 	' time unit where the original pays 100. `add_score` takes `#addv` in units
14786               	; 	' of ten (the prize beside it is `#addv = 5` for fifty points, and the bonus
14787               	; 	' Kop threshold is `#nextk = 1000` for ten thousand), so writing the band in
14788               	; 	' POINTS here shifted every tally one decimal place. Reported from play as
14789               	; 	' "it seems like you awarded 1000 per time unit left" -- exactly right.
14790               	; 	'
14791               	; 	' Nothing failed: 1,000 a unit is a plausible-looking number, the digits
14792               	; 	' all line up, and the only symptom is a score that runs away. The tell is
14793               	; 	' a constant written in a different unit from the routine it is passed to,
14794               	; 	' which is the same class of fault as the px-per-pass speeds in 3A.
14795               	; 	'
14796               	; 	' (This is also why the old comment here said "#bval MUST BE 16-BIT: 300
14797               	; 	' does not fit in a byte". At 10 / 20 / 30 it would, but it stays 16-bit
14798               	; 	' because `#addv` is, and a byte here would buy two bytes of ROM in
14799               	; 	' exchange for a truncation trap the next time somebody edits a band.)

14916               	;
14917               	; 	' AND IT ENDS ON ITS LAST BLIP -- there is no closing accent.
14918               	; 	'
14919               	; 	' Two were tried. The bench's own ending for this variant rose a fourth,
14920               	; 	' to 2,542 Hz, and a square wave there is a shriek -- the same fault the
14921               	; 	' pickup was rewritten for. Dropping it an OCTAVE BELOW the ticks, to
14922               	; 	' 518 Hz, was reported the same way, and that one cannot be too high by
14923               	; 	' any measure: it is the lowest note in the effect.
14924               	; 	'
14925               	; 	' So the complaint is not the pitch, it is the extra note. A tally is
14926               	; 	' arithmetic, and arithmetic finishes when the last term is added; a
14927               	; 	' flourish after it is a second event the player has to interpret, and
14928               	; 	' the HUD has already said the clock is empty. The count stops when the
14929               	; 	' counting stops.
14930               	;
14931               	; 	' `calc_bonus` USED TO LIVE HERE and computed the whole sum by repeated
14932               	; 	' addition, to dodge two hazards at once: `tsec * bmul` is an 8-bit
14933               	; 	' product (a 50-unit capture in the x300 band pays 15,000, six times past
14934               	; 	' a byte), and multiplying properly lands on the MPY/r0 hazard where a
14935               	; 	' 16-bit variable read straight after being multiplied returns the
14936               	; 	' product's high word. Counting the bonus out a unit at a time (above)
14937               	; 	' removes the multiply entirely rather than working around it -- the loop
14938               	; 	' the player watches IS the arithmetic.
14939               	; 	'
14940               	; 	' It also fixed the last-tick case for free: `bn_loop` tests `tsec = 0`
14941               	; 	' on entry, where the old `FOR bi = 1 TO tsec` would have run its body
14942               	; 	' once and paid a full multiplier for no time at all (CLAUDE.md 3A).
14943               	;

15242               	;
15243               	; 	' A SOUND STILL PLAYING WHEN THE ROUND ENDS IS ALLOWED TO FINISH.
15244               	; 	'
15245               	; 	' This used to open with a bare `GOSUB snd_off`, which cut it dead. That
15246               	; 	' was not an accident: the decay counters are ticked by the MAIN LOOP, and
15247               	; 	' this pause REPLACES the main loop, so a tone left latched with nothing
15248               	; 	' ticking it hangs for the full ninety frames -- the sticky-audio failure
15249               	; 	' this game has already shipped twice. The answer is to DRAIN the counters
15250               	; 	' rather than to stop silencing.
15251               	; 	'
15252               	; 	' CLEAR THE PENDING LATCHES FIRST. sf* flags are sounds that have not
15253               	; 	' happened yet; left set, the drain below would START one and the pause
15254               	; 	' would end with a fresh note ringing into the next round.
15255               	; 	'
15256               	; 	' THEN TICK sfx_tick WHOLE, not some decay-only part of it. The five
15257               	; 	' counters do not all live in one place: sot, sht and spt are a block at
15258               	; 	' the tail, but spz (the prize arpeggio) and swt (the jump warble) tick up
15259               	; 	' among the code that starts sounds. Draining only the tail would finish a
15260               	; 	' footstep and still cut the arpeggio, which is the one effect with a
15261               	; 	' phrase worth saving. Calling the whole routine also leaves the write
15262               	; 	' order on CHANNEL 2 alone, which spz and spt share.
15263               	; 	'
15264               	; 	' EVERY THIRD FRAME, because the main loop runs about 2.5 frames per pass
15265               	; 	' and this loop waits one frame per turn. Ticking every frame would play
15266               	; 	' everything at two and a half times its tuned speed. Three frames a tick
15267               	; 	' is ~17% slow and gives 30 ticks against the longest effect's 20 passes.
15268               	; 	'
15269               	; 	' THE LOOP COUNTS TICKS, NOT FRAMES, which is what makes the pacing free.
15270               	; 	' Counting 91 frames and firing on every third needs a second counter, an
15271               	; 	' increment and a test -- 48 bytes, on a fixed area with 66 left. Counting
15272               	; 	' 31 TICKS of three WAITs each is the same 93 frames and the same three
15273               	; 	' frames per tick, with none of that. The duration changes by two frames.
15274               	; 	'
15275               	; 	' snd_off still runs at the END, as the backstop for anything the drain
15276               	; 	' did not finish.
15277               	; pause_beat:

15640               	;
15641               	; 	' THE LOW-TIME WARNING IS SILENT. There was a beep a second under ten, and
15642               	; 	' it was the wrong instrument for the job: the last ten seconds are the
15643               	; 	' busiest part of a round, so a repeating tone arrives exactly when the
15644               	; 	' player most needs to hear the hazards, and it fought the prize arpeggio
15645               	; 	' for channel 2 as well. The flash says the same thing and says it in the
15646               	; 	' place the player is already looking.
15647               	;
15648               	; 	' FOOTSTEPS ARE NOISE, AND ON THE NOISE CHANNEL -- testsounds variant A.
15649               	; 	'
15650               	; 	' They were two alternating TONES on channel 0, which is neither what the
15651               	; 	' original does nor a good use of a channel: the recording says a footstep
15652               	; 	' is a short burst of white noise, and channel 3 was sitting unused while
15653               	; 	' the footsteps and the jump sweep shared channel 0 and had to take turns.
15654               	; 	'
15655               	; 	' TESTSOUNDS RUN D: a SHORT tick at the measured RATE.
15656               	; 	'
15657               	; 	' The two dials are independent and both were tried at the bench. The
15658               	; 	' 2600 plays a 64 ms burst every 165 ms -- six a second -- and variant A
15659               	; 	' copies both. Ten a second was tried on the way here and reads as
15660               	; 	' hurrying rather than running. What D changes is not the cadence but the
15661               	; 	' TICK: two frames rather than four, and a notch louder to carry at half
15662               	; 	' the length. Same six a second, less of it.
15663               	; 	'
15664               	; 	' EIGHT A SECOND, AND THE ACCUMULATOR NOW CARRIES ITS REMAINDER.
15665               	; 	'
15666               	; 	' sfw counted pixels and the trigger did `sfw = 0`, THROWING AWAY whatever
15667               	; 	' was past the threshold. kspd is about four pixels a pass, so a threshold
15668               	; 	' of 17 did not fire at 17 -- it fired at the first multiple past it, about
15669               	; 	' 20, and every rate this was ever set to came out slower than the number
15670               	; 	' said: the "six a second" was 5.2 and the "ten" that read as hurrying was
15671               	; 	' really 8.7. Subtracting the threshold instead keeps the fraction, so the
15672               	; 	' rate is what it claims to be at any walking speed.
15673               	; 	'
15674               	; 	' MEASURED OFF THE COLECOVISION: 14 px, about 7.4 a second.
15675               	; 	'
15676               	; 	' It was 15 px and 6.9 a second, picked between an 8.0 that read as
15677               	; 	' slightly hurried and a 6.1 that read as trudging -- a judgement between
15678               	; 	' two other judgements, with nothing underneath it. The ColecoVision
15679               	; 	' recording settles it: footfalls land every 0.130 s across a twelve-second
15680               	; 	' continuous run, which is 7.7 a second, and that is the one finding in the
15681               	; 	' whole sound analysis the method resolves EXACTLY -- a rhythm rather than a
15682               	; 	' pitch, counted off the RMS track rather than inferred from a spectrum.
15683               	; 	' (colecosounds variant 1A; assets/sfx/sfxref-coleco.md has the working.)
15684               	; 	'
15685               	; 	' 104 px/s over 14 px is 7.43 a second. 13 px would give 8.00, and 7.7 sits
15686               	; 	' almost exactly between them -- so this is the nearer of the two, and it is
15687               	; 	' also the one that does not walk back into the 8.0 that was rejected by ear.
15688               	; 	'
15689               	; 	' WHY THE GAME KEEPS A DISTANCE AND THE BENCH KEEPS A CADENCE. The bench
15690               	; 	' plays a fixed eight frames between steps because it has no walking to tie
15691               	; 	' them to; the game accumulates PIXELS TRAVELLED, so the feet keep time with
15692               	; 	' the legs when he is slowed or stopped. Matching "7.4 a second" therefore
15693               	; 	' means matching it AT HIS WALKING SPEED, and assumes the ColecoVision's
15694               	; 	' crook walks at ours -- which the recording cannot confirm.
15695               	; 	'
15696               	; 	' The dial is this one constant and the subtraction below, which must stay
15697               	; 	' threshold + 1 or the carry is wrong.
15698               	; 	'
15699               	; 	' SOT = 2 IS THE SHORTEST TICK THERE IS, and 1 is SILENCE. The decay block
15700               	; 	' below runs LATER IN THE SAME sfx_tick, so a count of 1 is decremented to
15701               	; 	' zero on the pass that set it and the note-off fires before the sound has
15702               	; 	' lasted any time at all. 2 survives to the next pass, which is one pass of
15703               	; 	' sound -- about 42 ms against the bench's 33, as close as a per-pass timer
15704               	; 	' gets, and the reason the bench and the game cannot sound identical.
15705               	; 	'
15706               	; 	' Register 4 is white noise at the fastest rate.
15707               	; 	'
15708               	; 	' VOLUME 9, WHICH IS UNDER EVERYTHING ELSE ON PURPOSE. The hit, the prize
15709               	; 	' and the jump are 12 and 13, and they happen ONCE; footsteps play for the

15913               	;
15914               	; 	' EVERYTHING BELOW THIS LINE IS ASSEMBLED INTO BANK 1, so the INCLUDE order
15915               	; 	' is load-bearing and nothing but data may follow it.
15916               	; 	'
15917               	; 	' THE FONT IS NOW IN THE BANK TOO, and it used to be deliberately outside:
15918               	; 	' keeping one readable thing in bank 0 means a bank-selection mistake shows
15919               	; 	' as "text survives, art does not" rather than a uniformly blank screen,
15920               	; 	' which is a genuinely useful thing to have when a bank goes wrong.
15921               	; 	'
15922               	; 	' THE FONT HAS A BANK OF ITS OWN, and the reason is not its size.
15923               	; 	'
15924               	; 	' Bank 1 was FULL -- six spare bytes of 8,192 -- which shut the door on
15925               	; 	' moving anything else out of the fixed area, and the fixed area is the
15926               	; 	' only budget that cannot be grown (linkticart writes exactly three
15927               	; 	' loader pages and discards the rest; they are the 32K expansion's RAM at
15928               	; 	' >A000, not cart ROM). A second bank costs a bigger cart -- five pages
15929               	; 	' round up to eight, so 32 KB becomes 64 KB -- and buys back the ability
15930               	; 	' to keep evacuating data out of code.
15931               	; 	'
15932               	; 	' THE FONT IS THE RIGHT TENANT because it is read ONCE. Two DEFINEs copy
15933               	; 	' it into VRAM at setup and nothing looks at it again, so it is the only
15934               	; 	' block here that can sit on a page which is not permanently mapped. See
15935               	; 	' setup_font: bank 2 is selected for those two statements and bank 1 for
15936               	; 	' the whole of the rest of the program.
15937               	; 	'
15938               	; 	' EVERYTHING ELSE STAYS IN BANK 1, because everything else is read during
15939               	; 	' play -- art on a screen crossing, templates on a band blit, the lookup
15940               	; 	' tables every pass. One permanently-mapped bank for all of it means
15941               	; 	' there is no switch to miss.
15942               	; 	#if TI994A
15943               	; 	BANK 2
15944      01EC     BANK_0_FREE:	EQU >fffe-$
